title: The Locality Trade-off in Masked Patch Self-Distillation
claim: Adding a masked-patch objective changes local patch similarity structure in a scale-dependent way that semantic masks alone cannot reveal.
layout: 2 rows by 6 columns, left-to-right, yellow anchor boxes on heatmaps
description: A 2-row by 6-column grid of images. Columns are labeled across the top: Image, Seg. mask, DINO ViT-B, DINO+iBOT ViT-B, DINO ViT-L, DINO+iBOT ViT-L. The top row shows a half-timbered brick building street scene. The bottom row shows a rugged canyon cliff landscape. The second column overlays semantic segmentation masks in pink and blue tints with white outlines, which mark coarse regions. The four right columns show jet-colored similarity heatmaps overlaid on the photo. Each has a yellow square marking the anchor patch, a window on the building and a cliff patch on the canyon. Red and yellow mean high similarity, and blue means low. The eye goes first to the bright heatmaps and yellow boxes, then compares how broad or focused the warm regions are across the models.
caption: Anchor-patch similarity heatmaps for DINO and DINO+iBOT on ADE20K examples, with semantic annotations shown for reference. Yellow boxes mark the anchor patches. For ViT-B, adding iBOT produces broader responses over the building and mountain, reducing distinctions associated with windows and rugged cliff structures. This effect is alleviated in ViT-L, where the +iBOT model also exhibits more spatially selective responses to these structures. The semantic masks do not resolve many of these within-region differences, illustrating why segmentation performance alone cannot characterize fine-grained local representations. Additional examples appear in Figure 10.
abstract: Masked patch self-distillation is a key component of modern vision foundation models, including DINOv2 and DINOv3, yet its implications for local visual information remain unclear. We show that its semantic benefits can coexist with a scale-dependent locality cost. Using two annotation-free diagnostics, we distinguish recoverable local appearance from spatial correspondence. In smaller models, adding iBOT substantially weakens patch correspondence while largely preserving appearance decodability. In larger models, correspondence improves, but pixel and texture evidence becomes less linearly accessible in deep features. Thus, scaling changes the form of the locality cost rather than uniformly eliminating it. Our analysis of Gram anchoring further shows that preserving patch relations does not guarantee simultaneous improvements in both properties. These findings motivate evaluating and designing visual representations around the complementary demands of semantic abstraction, appearance preservation, and spatial correspondence. Our code is available at https://github.com/winci-ai/jea.
